topics.title: Embeddings
topics.summary: What text embeddings are, how sentence-transformers turn sentences into vectors, and how to pick a model for RAG.
topics.whatIs:
An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. The sentence 'Abdur built a RAG chatbot for a real-estate company' becomes a vector of 384 floats. A different sentence with similar meaning, such as 'he developed a retrieval-based assistant for property listings', becomes a vector that sits close to the first one in that 384-dimensional space.

The model that produces these vectors is trained so that distance means semantic similarity, not keyword overlap. That is the whole trick: once text is a vector, 'find the paragraph that answers this question' becomes 'find the vector nearest to this one', which is plain arithmetic.

The model I use for this site is all-MiniLM-L6-v2 from the sentence-transformers library. It runs on CPU, loads in a couple of seconds, produces 384-dimensional vectors, and handles up to 256 word pieces per input. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small produces 1536 dimensions and is more accurate on long or technical text, but it costs money per call and needs a network round trip.
topics.why:
Keyword search fails the moment the user's words differ from the document's words. A recruiter asking 'has he done any work with vector databases?' would never match a paragraph that says 'LangChain + ChromaDB chatbot' with plain string matching. Embeddings close that gap because 'vector databases' and 'ChromaDB' land near each other in the vector space.

Every RAG system, semantic search feature, recommendation engine and clustering job starts with embeddings. If the embeddings are poor, nothing downstream can fix it, so understanding what they are and what they cannot do is the first real AI-engineering skill.
how: Load an embedding model once at startup. Loading per request is the most common performance bug I see in beginner code.
Call model.encode() on a list of strings. Batching is much faster than encoding one string at a time.
Each string becomes a fixed-length vector regardless of its length; a 5-word sentence and a 200-word paragraph both become 384 numbers.
Normalize the vectors (unit length) so cosine similarity reduces to a dot product. sentence-transformers can do this with normalize_embeddings=True.
Store the vectors next to the original text. You retrieve by vector but you show, and feed the LLM, the original text.
Always embed queries with the same model that embedded the documents. Vectors from two different models are not comparable.
topics.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

# Load once, reuse for every request (this takes ~2s, encoding takes ~ms)
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

sentences = [
    "Abdur built a RAG chatbot with LangChain and ChromaDB.",
    "He developed a retrieval-based assistant for property listings.",
    "The recipe needs two eggs and a cup of flour.",
]

# normalize_embeddings=True gives unit vectors, so dot product == cosine
vectors = model.encode(sentences, normalize_embeddings=True)
print(vectors.shape)  # (3, 384)

# Compare the first sentence with the other two
for i in (1, 2):
    score = float(np.dot(vectors[0], vectors[i]))
    print(f"similarity(0, {i}) = {score:.3f}")

# Typical output: ~0.6 for the paraphrase, ~0.05 for the recipe
pitfalls: Mixing models: embedding documents with one model and queries with another gives meaningless similarity scores.
Ignoring the token limit: MiniLM silently truncates after 256 word pieces, so the end of a long paragraph is never seen. Chunk first.
Embedding on every request: the model load belongs at startup, not inside the endpoint.

Expecting exact matches: embeddings capture meaning, so 'Python developer' and 'Django engineer' score high, but a product code like 'SKU-4471' will not retrieve reliably. Use keyword search for that.
Treating the dimension count as quality: 1536 dimensions is not automatically better than 384. Benchmark on your own data.
useCases: Semantic search over documentation, tickets or a knowledge base
The retrieval step of every RAG pipeline
Deduplication and clustering of similar records
Recommendations: 'users who read this also read' without any user history
Classification by nearest labelled example when you have little training data

qa.q: What does an embedding actually represent?
qa.a: A point in a high-dimensional space where distance reflects meaning. Two texts that say similar things, even with different words, end up close together. The individual numbers have no human-readable meaning; only the geometry matters.

qa.q: Why use a local model like all-MiniLM-L6-v2 instead of the OpenAI embedding API?
qa.a: It is free, runs on CPU in milliseconds, keeps data on your own server and has no network dependency. For a small knowledge base like a portfolio it retrieves just as well. I would switch to a hosted model when the corpus is large, multilingual or highly technical and recall measurably improves.

qa.q: Can you compare embeddings from two different models?
qa.a: No. Each model defines its own space. A vector from MiniLM and a vector from text-embedding-3-small are different lengths and have unrelated axes. If you change the embedding model you must re-embed the entire corpus.

qa.q: What is the difference between a word embedding and a sentence embedding?
qa.a: Word embeddings like word2vec give one vector per word with no context, so 'bank' is the same vector in 'river bank' and 'bank account'. Sentence embeddings from transformer models encode the whole input, so context changes the vector. RAG uses sentence or passage embeddings.

qa.q: How do you decide the embedding model for a project?
qa.a: Build a small test set of real questions with the chunk that should be retrieved, then measure recall at k for two or three candidate models. Also weigh latency, cost, token limit and whether the data can leave your server. The MTEB leaderboard is a starting point, not an answer.

qa.q: Why normalize embeddings?
qa.a: With unit-length vectors, cosine similarity equals the dot product, which is faster and lets you use plain matrix multiplication or any vector index in inner-product mode. It also removes the effect of text length on vector magnitude.

topics.usedIn: This portfolio's chatbot embeds knowledge_base.txt once at startup with sentence-transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) and keeps the vectors in memory as a NumPy matrix, so every question is answered against my real career data in a few milliseconds of retrieval time.

topics.title: Chunking Strategy
topics.summary: How to split documents into chunks for RAG: paragraph vs fixed-size vs recursive splitting, overlap, and the self-contained rule.
topics.whatIs:
Chunking is splitting a document into smaller pieces before embedding them. Each piece, or chunk, becomes one row in your vector store and is the unit you retrieve. The chunk is what the LLM eventually reads, so its boundaries decide whether the model sees a complete fact or half of one.

There is no single correct chunk size. A legal contract, a Slack export and a resume need different strategies. The decision that matters is: when a chunk is pulled out on its own, with no neighbours, does it still make sense and still answer a question?

For this site I chose paragraph chunks. Every paragraph in my knowledge base is one complete idea: one job, one project, one skill group. That made the self-contained rule easy to satisfy and gave me 50-odd clean chunks instead of hundreds of fragments.
topics.why:
If the whole document is one chunk, retrieval returns everything every time, the prompt fills with irrelevant text, cost goes up and the model gets distracted. If chunks are too small, a fact gets cut in half and the retrieved piece says 'he worked there for two years' with no mention of where.

Chunking also sets your retrieval precision ceiling. The embedding of a chunk is an average of everything in it, so a chunk that mixes three topics has a blurry vector that matches none of them well. Clean chunks produce sharp vectors.
how: Paragraph splitting: split on blank lines. Works when the author already wrote one idea per paragraph, which is true for resumes, FAQs and most documentation.
Fixed-size splitting: cut every N characters or tokens, typically 300 to 800 tokens. Simple and predictable, but it ignores structure and cuts mid-sentence.

Recursive splitting: try to split on headings, then paragraphs, then sentences, then characters, until every piece is under the size limit. This is what LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter does and it is the sensible default for mixed documents.
Overlap: repeat the last 10 to 20 percent of one chunk at the start of the next, so a sentence that straddles a boundary appears whole in at least one chunk.
Make chunks self-contained: replace pronouns with names ('Abdur led the migration' instead of 'he led the migration') and keep the entity being described inside each chunk.
Add metadata: store the source file, heading and position with each chunk so you can filter, cite and debug retrieval later.
topics.code:
import re

def paragraph_chunks(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """One chunk per paragraph. Used for the portfolio knowledge base."""
    return [p.strip() for p in text.split("\n\n") if p.strip()]

def fixed_chunks(text: str, size: int = 500, overlap: int = 80) -> list[str]:
    """Fixed-size character windows with overlap, snapped to sentence ends."""
    sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text)
    chunks, current = [], ""
    for s in sentences:
        if len(current) + len(s) > size and current:
            chunks.append(current.strip())
            current = current[-overlap:]  # carry the tail forward
        current += " " + s
    if current.strip():
        chunks.append(current.strip())
    return chunks

doc = open("knowledge_base.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
paras = paragraph_chunks(doc)
fixed = fixed_chunks(doc)
print(len(paras), "paragraph chunks;", len(fixed), "fixed chunks")
print(paras[0][:120])
pitfalls: Cutting mid-sentence or mid-table so the retrieved chunk is grammatically broken and the LLM has to guess the missing half.
Pronouns everywhere: a chunk that says 'it reduced costs by 30%' is useless on its own because 'it' is in the previous chunk.
Chunks that are too big: a 2000-token chunk has a vague embedding and wastes the context window on text that is mostly irrelevant.
Forgetting that the embedding model truncates: a 600-word chunk fed to MiniLM only has its first ~200 words embedded.
Never re-checking after the source changes: a new document format can silently break the splitter and produce one giant chunk.
useCases: Preparing any long document (resume, manual, policy, contract) for RAG
Splitting PDFs or web articles into searchable units
Building a support knowledge base from existing help-centre articles
Indexing code repositories by function or class rather than by file

qa.q: What is the trade-off in choosing chunk size?
qa.a: Small chunks give precise retrieval but can lose context, so an answer needs several of them. Large chunks keep context but have blurry embeddings and pull irrelevant text into the prompt. Most teams land between 200 and 500 words and then tune using a retrieval test set.

qa.q: What does it mean for a chunk to be self-contained?
qa.a: That a reader given only that chunk could answer a question about it without the surrounding text. In practice: full names instead of pronouns, the subject stated in each chunk, no 'as mentioned above'. This single rule fixed more retrieval misses for me than any model change.

qa.q: Why use overlap between chunks?
qa.a: So that a sentence or fact that lands on a boundary is present in full in at least one chunk. The cost is some duplicated text in the index. Paragraph chunking usually does not need overlap because paragraph boundaries are already natural breaks.

qa.q: How would you chunk a document with headings and tables?
qa.a: Split by heading first so every chunk belongs to one section, prepend the heading text to each chunk so the context travels with it, and keep tables whole or convert each row into a sentence. Recursive splitting with a size cap handles the rest.

qa.q: How do you know your chunking is good?
qa.a: Measure it. Write 20 to 30 real questions, note which chunk should answer each, and check how often that chunk appears in the top k. Change the strategy and re-run. Looking at a few results by hand is not evaluation.

qa.q: Should chunk size depend on the embedding model?
qa.a: Yes. Every embedding model has a maximum input length, and quality degrades before that limit. MiniLM handles 256 word pieces, roughly 200 English words, so chunks larger than that lose their tail. Larger-context models like text-embedding-3 allow bigger chunks.

topics.usedIn: The portfolio backend splits knowledge_base.txt on blank lines, so each paragraph (one job, one project, one skill group) becomes a chunk. Paragraph chunks worked better than fixed-size windows because each fact stays intact and every chunk already names the subject.

topics.title: Cosine Similarity & Semantic Search
topics.summary: How cosine similarity scores two embeddings, why it beats Euclidean distance for text, and how semantic search uses it.
topics.whatIs:
Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors. If they point in the same direction the score is 1, if they are perpendicular it is 0, and if they point in opposite directions it is -1. For text embeddings, a score near 1 means 'these two texts mean nearly the same thing'.

It ignores vector length and only looks at direction. That matters because the magnitude of an embedding can drift with input length or repetition, while the direction carries the meaning. Two paragraphs about Django deployment point the same way whether one is 30 words and the other 300.

Semantic search is just cosine similarity applied at scale: embed the query, compute the score against every stored vector, sort descending, take the top results. With normalized vectors that is a single matrix multiplication, which is why a NumPy array can serve retrieval for thousands of chunks in under a millisecond.
topics.why:
Retrieval needs a number that says how relevant a chunk is to a question. Cosine similarity is that number. It is cheap, works well for high-dimensional embeddings, and most embedding models are trained with it as the objective, so it is the metric their geometry was shaped for.

Understanding it also tells you what the scores mean and do not mean. A 0.42 is not 'forty-two percent relevant'; it is only comparable to other scores from the same model. That understanding stops you from hard-coding a threshold that works for one model and silently breaks for another.
how: Formula: cos(a, b) = (a · b) / (||a|| × ||b||). The dot product divided by the product of the lengths.
With unit-length vectors the denominator is 1, so cosine similarity equals the dot product. Normalize once at indexing time and skip the division forever.
For a query against N chunks, stack the chunk vectors into an N × d matrix and compute matrix @ query. The result is N scores in one operation.
np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:k] gives the indices of the k highest-scoring chunks.
Scores are relative: compare them against each other within one model, not against a universal threshold.
Beyond a few hundred thousand vectors, brute force gets slow and you move to an approximate index (HNSW in FAISS, Qdrant, pgvector or Chroma).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

chunks = [
    "Abdur migrated Django monoliths to FastAPI microservices on AWS.",
    "He built a LangChain and ChromaDB chatbot for a real-estate company.",
    "Lahore is the capital of Punjab province in Pakistan.",
]
# Index once: unit vectors so dot product == cosine similarity
index = model.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True)

def search(query: str, k: int = 2):
    q = model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    scores = index @ q                      # one score per chunk
    top = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:k]      # highest first
    return [(chunks[i], round(float(scores[i]), 3)) for i in top]

for text, score in search("any experience with vector databases?"):
    print(score, text)

# The ChromaDB chunk should rank first even though the query never
# says 'ChromaDB': that is semantic search.
pitfalls: Using Euclidean distance on unnormalized embeddings and wondering why long chunks always lose.
Hard-coding a threshold like 'only keep chunks above 0.7'. Score distributions differ per model; set thresholds from your own data or skip them.
Recomputing the chunk embeddings on every query. Encode once, store, reuse.
Comparing a query vector to chunk vectors from a different model: the scores are random noise.
Assuming the top score is always relevant. If nothing in the corpus matches, the top result is still returned; check the score gap or let the LLM say 'not found'.
useCases: The retrieval step in RAG
Finding duplicate tickets, questions or product listings
'Related articles' and 'similar items' features
Matching candidate resumes against a job description
Clustering feedback or reviews by topic

qa.q: Why cosine similarity instead of Euclidean distance?
qa.a: Cosine ignores magnitude and compares direction only, and in text embeddings direction carries the meaning. Euclidean distance is also affected by vector length, so longer or denser inputs can look 'farther' even when they mean the same thing. Most embedding models are trained with a cosine objective, so it matches their geometry.

qa.q: What does a cosine similarity of 0.8 mean?
qa.a: Within one model, that the two texts are closely related in meaning. It is not a percentage and it is not comparable across models. For MiniLM, paraphrases often score 0.6 to 0.9 while unrelated text sits near 0 to 0.2.

qa.q: How does semantic search differ from keyword search?
qa.a: Keyword search matches the literal words, so 'vector database' misses a document that only says 'ChromaDB'. Semantic search compares meaning via embeddings, so it finds that document. Keyword search still wins for exact identifiers, names and codes, which is why production systems often combine both.

qa.q: How do you make cosine search fast for millions of vectors?
qa.a: Brute force is O(N × d) per query, fine up to a few hundred thousand vectors in NumPy. Past that you use an approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW, which trades a small loss in recall for sub-millisecond queries. Vector databases wrap exactly this.

qa.q: If vectors are normalized, why do libraries still offer a cosine metric?
qa.a: Convenience and safety. Not every caller normalizes, so the library computes the full formula. If you know your vectors are unit length, dot product gives the same ranking faster.

qa.q: What happens when the query is unrelated to everything in the index?
qa.a: You still get a top result, just with a low score. A robust system notices that the best score is far below the usual range or that the gap between the top results is tiny, and either asks the user to rephrase or tells the LLM the context may not contain the answer.

topics.usedIn: In main.py the visitor's question is embedded and compared against every chunk with scikit-learn's cosine_similarity. The highest-scoring chunks become the context the LLM answers from. With only a few dozen chunks, brute-force NumPy comparison is faster than any vector database round trip.

topics.title: Top-K Retrieval
topics.summary: How to choose k in RAG retrieval, why top-5 beat top-3 for this site, and when thresholds, filters and reranking help.
topics.whatIs:
Top-k retrieval returns the k best-scoring chunks for a query instead of only the single best one. If k is 5, the five most similar chunks are concatenated into the prompt. The idea is that the right answer is usually near the top of the ranking but not always exactly at the top, and that many questions need more than one chunk to answer.

k is a dial between recall and noise. Larger k means more chance the needed chunk is included, but also more irrelevant text in the prompt, higher token cost and more opportunity for the model to be distracted by a near-miss.

On this site the first endpoint used k = 3. When I built the chat endpoint I raised it to 5 because questions like 'what has he done with AWS?' touch several jobs at once, and three chunks kept missing one of them.
topics.why:
A single chunk rarely contains the full answer to a multi-part question. 'Where has Abdur worked and what did he build there?' spans five employer paragraphs. At the same time, dumping the whole knowledge base into every prompt wastes tokens and buries the signal. Top-k is the practical middle: enough context to answer, little enough to stay focused.

Getting k right is also one of the cheapest quality improvements available. It is a one-line change that you can evaluate in minutes, unlike swapping the embedding model or re-chunking everything.
how: Score every chunk against the query (cosine similarity), sort descending and keep the first k.
Start with k between 3 and 5 for small corpora with clean chunks; go to 8 to 10 when chunks are small or questions are broad.
Make k depend on chunk size: five 500-word chunks is 2500 words of context, five 100-word chunks is 500.
Add a minimum-score cutoff only after inspecting real score distributions; a fixed threshold from a blog post will not match your model.
Filter before ranking when you have metadata: restrict to the right document, date range or tenant, then take top k inside that subset.
For larger corpora, retrieve a generous candidate set (k = 20) and rerank with a cross-encoder down to the 3 to 5 you actually send to the LLM.
pitfalls: Picking k once and never measuring it again after the knowledge base grows or the chunking changes.
Setting k so high that the prompt exceeds the model's useful attention. Models answer worse when the relevant chunk is buried in the middle of a long context.
Treating k as the only knob. Chunk quality and the embedding model matter more than k = 3 versus k = 4.
Returning top k even when every score is terrible, so the LLM confidently answers from unrelated text.
Sending the chunks in random order. Put the highest-scoring chunk first; models weight the start of the context more.
useCases: Every RAG prompt assembly step
Search result pages that show the best N matches
Candidate generation before a reranking stage
Few-shot example selection: pick the k most similar labelled examples for the prompt

qa.q: How do you choose k?
qa.a: Measure recall at k on a test set of real questions: for each question, is the chunk that answers it inside the top k? Pick the smallest k where recall stops improving. For this site that was 5. Then sanity-check the token count of k chunks against the model's context and your cost budget.

qa.q: What is the downside of a large k?
qa.a: Token cost, latency and distraction. Irrelevant chunks give the model text to be wrong with, and long contexts suffer from the 'lost in the middle' effect where facts in the centre of the prompt are used less reliably than facts at the start or end.

qa.q: Should you use a similarity threshold instead of a fixed k?
qa.a: Usually both: top k with a floor. A pure threshold returns zero results for hard questions and fifty for easy ones. A pure k returns garbage when nothing matches. Set the floor from the score distribution of your own queries, not from a number you read somewhere.

qa.q: What is reranking and when do you add it?
qa.a: A second, more expensive model scores query and chunk together and reorders the candidates. You retrieve a wide set with cheap embeddings, say 20, then rerank down to 5. It is worth adding when the corpus is large or when the right chunk is often ranked 4th to 10th by embeddings alone.

qa.q: How does metadata filtering interact with top k?
qa.a: Filter first, rank second. If the user asks about 2024 work, restrict candidates to chunks tagged 2024, then take the top k of those. Ranking first and filtering after can leave you with fewer than k results or none at all.

qa.q: Why did this site move from top-3 to top-5?
qa.a: Multi-part questions about several employers or several technologies kept missing one relevant paragraph at k = 3. Five chunks of one paragraph each is under a thousand tokens, so the cost increase was negligible and the misses stopped.

topics.usedIn: The portfolio chat retrieves the top 5 chunks per question; the simpler /ask endpoint uses top 3. Five was enough to cover multi-part questions like 'what has he built with AWS?' without stuffing the prompt with unrelated facts. Each chunk is one paragraph, so five chunks stay under a thousand tokens.

topics.title: RAG Pipeline (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
topics.summary: How a RAG pipeline works end to end: chunk, embed, retrieve, build the prompt, generate. With the FastAPI code behind this site.
topics.whatIs:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation is an architecture where the model is handed the relevant facts at question time instead of being expected to remember them. The pipeline retrieves the most relevant pieces of your own data, puts them into the prompt, and only then asks the LLM to answer.

The LLM never learns your data. It reads it, the same way you would read a reference page before answering a question in an open-book exam. Change the data and the next answer reflects the change immediately, with no retraining.

This site is a RAG product. The knowledge base is a plain text file about my career. A FastAPI backend embeds it at startup, retrieves the five most relevant paragraphs for each visitor question, and asks gpt-4o-mini to answer from them, returning JSON that also tells the React frontend which card to display.
topics.why:
LLMs have a training cutoff, know nothing about private data and will confidently invent details when asked about things they have not seen. Fine-tuning does not fix that: it changes style and behaviour, not reliable recall of facts, and it has to be repeated every time the data changes.

RAG is the standard answer to 'make the model answer from our documents'. It is cheaper than fine-tuning, updates instantly, lets you show sources, and keeps the data on your side of the API boundary. Almost every production LLM feature that touches company data is some form of RAG.
how: Index time: split the source into chunks, embed each chunk, store vectors alongside the text. Do this once at startup or whenever the data changes.
Query time, step 1: embed the user's question with the same model.
Step 2 (Retrieval): score the question against every chunk and keep the top k.
Step 3 (Augmentation): build a prompt that contains the retrieved chunks, clear instructions and the question.
Step 4 (Generation): send the prompt to the LLM and return its answer, ideally with the chunks it used as sources.
Wrap it in a fallback: if the LLM call fails, return a keyword-based answer or a graceful message rather than a 500.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from openai import OpenAI

app = FastAPI()
client = OpenAI()
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

# --- index time: once at startup ---
text = open("knowledge_base.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
chunks = [p.strip() for p in text.split("\n\n") if p.strip()]
index = model.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True)

class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str

@app.post("/ask")
def ask(req: Ask):
    # --- query time ---
    q = model.encode([req.question], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    top = np.argsort(index @ q)[::-1][:5]                 # retrieval
    context = "\n\n".join(chunks[i] for i in top)
    prompt = ("Answer only from the context below. If the answer is not "
              f"there, say so.\n\nContext:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {req.question}")
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(                 # generation
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    return {"answer": reply.choices[0].message.content,
            "sources": [chunks[i] for i in top]}
pitfalls: No instruction to stay inside the context, so the model blends retrieved facts with its own guesses and you cannot tell which is which.
Embedding the knowledge base inside the request handler instead of at startup, making every call seconds slower.
Returning answers without sources. Sources are how you debug retrieval and how users learn to trust the system.
Testing with three questions you wrote yourself. Real users phrase things differently; collect their questions and build a test set.
No fallback path. When the LLM provider has an outage your whole product goes down with it.
useCases: Customer support assistants grounded in help-centre articles
Internal knowledge search over wikis, tickets and documents
Portfolio and resume assistants like this one
Contract and policy Q&A where every answer must cite its source
Product assistants that read live catalogue data

qa.q: When is RAG better than fine-tuning?
qa.a: When the data changes, when you need citations, when you cannot afford training runs or when the facts are private. Fine-tuning is for changing how the model writes or behaves, such as tone, format or a specialised task, not for teaching it a document collection that updates weekly. Many production systems use both: fine-tune for style, RAG for facts.

qa.q: How does RAG reduce hallucination?
qa.a: The model is told to answer from supplied text rather than from memory, and that text contains the real facts. It does not eliminate hallucination: the model can still misread the context or answer from memory when retrieval misses. Good instructions, strong retrieval and evaluation close that gap.

qa.q: Walk me through what happens when a user sends a question to this site.
qa.a: The React frontend posts the question and chat history to /api/chat. FastAPI embeds the question with MiniLM, scores it against the pre-embedded paragraphs with cosine similarity, and takes the top five. Those paragraphs go into a system prompt with rules about the JSON format. gpt-4o-mini returns an intent label and the answer text, and the frontend uses the intent to render a matching card.

qa.q: Where does a RAG system usually fail?
qa.a: Retrieval, far more often than generation. If the right chunk is not in the top k, the best model in the world cannot answer correctly. So when an answer is wrong, I check the retrieved chunks first, then the chunking, then the prompt, and only then the model.

qa.q: How do you keep the knowledge base up to date?
qa.a: For a text file, re-embed at startup and redeploy, which is what this site does. For larger systems, embed on write: when a document changes, re-chunk and upsert its vectors with the document id as the key, so stale chunks are replaced rather than duplicated.

qa.q: What would you improve first in a naive RAG pipeline?
qa.a: Add an evaluation set, then hybrid retrieval. Naive cosine top-k misses exact terms like product codes and names, and a BM25 keyword pass combined with the embedding pass fixes most of those misses. After that, a reranker and query rewriting for follow-up questions.

qa.q: How do you handle a question the knowledge base cannot answer?
qa.a: Instruct the model to say so and point to a real contact channel, and make sure the test set includes such questions so you catch regressions. On this site the prompt says never to invent employers, dates or links, and the fallback responder answers from the same real data.

topics.usedIn: This whole site is a RAG product: FastAPI retrieves the most relevant chunks, injects them into the system prompt, and gpt-4o-mini returns a JSON reply with an intent label so the React frontend can render the matching visual component. If OpenAI is unavailable, a keyword responder answers from the same data.
