It speaks as the AI voice of Abdur, grounded in the same knowledge base as this site, with a hard session timer as a cost guard.

topics.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
topics.summary: What MCP is, how servers expose tools and resources to any AI client, and how to write a server in Python with FastMCP.
topics.whatIs:
The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server exposes capabilities, mainly tools the model can call and resources it can read. An MCP client, such as Claude Desktop, Claude Code, an IDE or your own agent, connects to the server, lists what it offers and makes those tools available to the model.

Before MCP every integration was bespoke: your agent had its own code for Slack, its own for Postgres, its own for the file system, and none of it worked in any other agent. With MCP you write the Slack server once and every MCP-capable client can use it. It is to AI tools what USB was to peripherals.

Under the hood it is JSON-RPC over either standard input and output (for local servers launched as a subprocess) or HTTP (for remote servers). The official Python SDK includes FastMCP, which turns a decorated function into a tool with its schema generated from the type hints.
topics.why:
Agents are only as useful as the tools they can reach, and hand-wiring every tool into every agent does not scale. MCP separates the two: tool builders ship servers, agent builders pick servers. A company can expose its internal systems once and let every AI assistant in the building use them with the same permissions and logging.

For an AI engineer it is now table stakes. Clients ask for 'an MCP server for our API' the way they used to ask for a REST API, and knowing how tools, resources and transports fit together is the difference between integrating in an afternoon and reinventing a protocol.
how: A server declares tools (functions with a name, description and JSON Schema input), resources (readable data addressed by URI, like files or records) and prompts (reusable templates).
The client starts or connects to the server, calls list_tools, and converts the returned schemas into function-calling tools for the model.
When the model requests a tool, the client sends call_tool over JSON-RPC, the server runs the function and returns the result, and the client feeds it back to the model.
Local servers use stdio: the client launches the server as a subprocess and talks over pipes. Remote servers use streamable HTTP with authentication.
Permissions live in the client. A good client asks the user before running a tool with side effects and logs every call.
Write tool descriptions as documentation for the model: when to use the tool, what it returns and what it must not be used for.
topics.code:
# portfolio_mcp.py: expose the portfolio knowledge base to any MCP client
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

mcp = FastMCP("abdur-portfolio")
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
chunks = [p.strip() for p in open("knowledge_base.txt", encoding="utf-8")
          .read().split("\n\n") if p.strip()]
index = model.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True)

@mcp.tool()
def search_portfolio(query: str, k: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    """Search Abdur Rehman Afzal's career knowledge base.
    Use this before answering any question about his experience,
    projects, skills or certifications. Returns the top-k paragraphs."""
    q = model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    top = np.argsort(index @ q)[::-1][:k]
    return [chunks[i] for i in top]

@mcp.resource("portfolio://knowledge-base")
def knowledge_base() -> str:
    """The full knowledge base as plain text."""
    return "\n\n".join(chunks)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()   # stdio transport; a client launches this file as a subprocess

# Claude Desktop config: {"mcpServers": {"portfolio":
#   {"command": "python", "args": ["portfolio_mcp.py"]}}}
pitfalls: Exposing dangerous operations as tools without the client confirming. Delete, pay and send should require a human in the loop.
Returning huge payloads. A tool that dumps a whole database table into the context wastes tokens and confuses the model. Paginate and summarise.
Vague descriptions. The model picks tools by reading them; 'query' is useless, 'search Abdur's career knowledge base, call before answering career questions' works.
Trusting tool output as instructions. Text returned from a tool is data; a document that says 'ignore your rules' is a prompt injection through the tool channel.
Running remote servers without authentication. An HTTP MCP server is an API; secure it like one.
useCases: Giving Claude Desktop or Claude Code access to an internal API, database or knowledge base
Shipping one integration that works across several AI assistants
Letting a company's agents share a vetted, logged set of tools
Exposing a RAG index so any client can search it
Wrapping legacy systems so models can read from them safely

qa.q: What problem does MCP solve?
qa.a: The N-times-M integration problem: every agent needing custom code for every tool. MCP standardises how a client discovers and calls tools, so a server written once works with any compliant client. It also centralises permissions and logging in the client instead of scattering them across integrations.

qa.q: How is MCP different from function calling?
qa.a: Function calling is how a model requests a tool within one API call. MCP is how an application finds and connects to tool servers. The client takes the tools an MCP server advertises and presents them to the model as function-calling tools, so MCP sits one layer above function calling.

qa.q: What are tools, resources and prompts in MCP?
qa.a: Tools are functions the model can invoke with arguments. Resources are data the client can read and attach to the context, addressed by URI, like a file or a database row. Prompts are reusable templates the server offers, such as 'summarise this ticket'. Most servers only need tools.

qa.q: stdio or HTTP transport?
qa.a: stdio for local servers: the client launches the process and talks over pipes, no network, no auth needed, ideal for developer tools. HTTP for shared or remote servers that several clients use, with proper authentication. Same protocol, different plumbing.

qa.q: How do you secure an MCP server?
qa.a: Keep side-effecting tools behind client confirmation, validate every argument, scope credentials to the least access the tools need, log every call with its arguments, and authenticate HTTP transports. Treat anything returned from external data as untrusted text, never as instructions.

qa.q: How would you expose this portfolio over MCP?
qa.a: A FastMCP server with one tool, search_portfolio, that runs the same embedding retrieval as the site, plus a resource for the full knowledge base. A recruiter using Claude Desktop could add it and ask questions about my work directly, with answers grounded in the same data as the chatbot.

topics.title: System Prompt Design for Products
topics.summary: How to write a production system prompt: role, context, output contract, rules and examples, with the prompt behind this site as the example.
topics.whatIs:
The system prompt is the standing instruction set your application sends with every request. It defines who the model is, what it knows, what format it must reply in, and what it must never do. In a product it is code, not prose: it is versioned, tested and reviewed like any other code path, because a one-word change can alter every response.

A good production prompt has a predictable structure. Role and scope first. Then the injected context, such as retrieved chunks. Then the output contract, ideally a JSON schema. Then behavioural rules, from most to least important. Then edge-case handling and style rules. The order matters because models weight the start and the end of the prompt most.

The prompt behind this site's chat follows that structure. It names the assistant, injects the retrieved knowledge-base excerpts, demands JSON with an intent field and an answer, then lists rules for each intent, including a fixed sentence for contact requests, a ban on invented employers or dates, and a style rule about punctuation.
topics.why:
The prompt is the cheapest lever in the whole system. Changing a model costs money and migration; changing chunking means re-indexing; changing a rule in the prompt takes thirty seconds and affects every answer immediately. That power cuts both ways, which is why prompts need the same discipline as code.

It is also where product behaviour lives. The decision that a 'contact' question renders a card instead of a paragraph, that answers stay under three sentences unless the question is technical, that the bot redirects off-topic questions politely: all of that is prompt design, and it is what the user actually experiences.
how: Role and scope: one or two sentences stating who the model is and what it is for. 'You are Abdur's portfolio assistant. Answer questions about his career from the excerpts below.'
Context slot: a clearly delimited block for retrieved text, with a label so the model knows it is reference material, not instructions.
Output contract: the exact format, as a schema. If the frontend reads a field, define it here and enforce it with structured output.
Rules in priority order, phrased as positive instructions where possible. 'Keep replies under three sentences' beats 'do not be verbose'.
Edge cases with explicit handling: what to say when the answer is not in the context, how to treat off-topic questions, what to do with contact requests.
Keep it under control: every rule should exist because a test case failed without it. Delete rules that no longer earn their place.
topics.code:
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are Abdur Rehman Afzal's AI Portfolio Assistant. Answer
questions about Abdur using only the Knowledge Base excerpts below, and
decide which UI component the frontend should render.

Knowledge Base (most relevant excerpts for this question):
======================
{knowledge_base}
======================

Respond with valid JSON matching exactly:
{{"intent": "me" | "projects" | "resume" | "skills" | "contact" | "general",
  "ai_text": "your conversational reply"}}

Rules:
- "me" for introductions. The frontend shows a profile card, so do not
  repeat his bio; write one friendly line that invites a question.
- "projects" only when the user asks to see or list projects. Follow-up
  questions about one project are "general".
- "contact" when the user wants to reach him. Set ai_text to EXACTLY:
  "You can reach Abdur through the contact info above. What's on your mind?"
- Keep ai_text under 3 sentences unless the question is technical; then
  use 1-2 short paragraphs with bullets where helpful.
- Never invent employers, dates, links or certifications not in the
  excerpts. If unsure, say so and point to a real contact channel.
- Never use em dashes. Use commas, colons or periods.
"""

def build_messages(chunks: list[str], history: list[dict], question: str):
    system = SYSTEM_PROMPT.format(knowledge_base="\n\n".join(chunks))
    return ([{"role": "system", "content": system}]
            + history[-16:]
            + [{"role": "user", "content": question}])
pitfalls: Rules written as a wish list with no tests behind them. If you cannot show the case a rule fixes, you cannot tell when it stops working.
Burying the output format in the middle. Put the contract near the top and enforce it with JSON mode or a schema, not with hope.
Negative-only instructions. Models follow 'do X' more reliably than 'never do Y'; where you need a ban, pair it with what to do instead.
Letting retrieved context and instructions blur together. Delimit the context block clearly or a document can hijack the prompt.
Editing the prompt in production without a changelog. Version it, diff it and run the evaluation set before deploying.
useCases: Chat assistants whose replies drive UI components
Support bots with strict scope and escalation rules
Extraction and classification tasks with fixed output schemas
Voice agents where reply length and tone must be tightly controlled
Any LLM feature that must behave the same way for every user

qa.q: What goes in a system prompt versus the user message?
qa.a: The system prompt holds everything that is true for every request: role, rules, format, and injected reference context. The user message holds this request's content. Mixing them makes rules easy to override and hard to test, and some models weight system instructions more heavily.

qa.q: How do you stop the model repeating information the UI already shows?
qa.a: Tell it what the UI will render for each intent and instruct it to complement, not duplicate. On this site, the 'me' intent triggers a profile card, so the prompt says not to repeat the bio and to write one inviting line instead. Without that rule the answer and the card said the same thing.

qa.q: Why force a fixed sentence for the contact intent?
qa.a: Consistency and safety. The contact card already shows the real details, so the text only needs to point at it, and pinning the sentence means the model can never paraphrase a phone number wrongly or invent an email. Fixed strings for high-stakes replies are a cheap guardrail.

qa.q: How long should a system prompt be?
qa.a: As short as the test set allows. Every rule costs tokens on every call and competes for the model's attention. I add a rule only when a test case fails without it and remove rules that no longer change any output. Hundreds of words is normal; thousands is a sign the task should be split.

qa.q: How do you test a prompt change?
qa.a: Run the evaluation set before and after: the same questions, compared on intent accuracy, keyword hits, faithfulness and length. Look at the diffs, not just the averages. For this site the set includes greetings, each intent, follow-ups and off-topic questions so a change to one rule cannot silently break another.

qa.q: Should few-shot examples go in the system prompt?
qa.a: When the format or tone is hard to describe, yes, two or three short examples beat paragraphs of rules. Keep them realistic and keep them updated when the rules change; a stale example contradicts the instructions and the model follows the example.

topics.usedIn: The system prompt behind this site's chat injects the five retrieved paragraphs, demands JSON with an intent field, maps each intent to the card the React frontend renders, pins the contact reply to a fixed sentence, bans invented facts and even sets a punctuation rule. Every rule in it exists because an earlier version got that case wrong.

topics.title: Evaluating LLM Apps (Golden Sets & LLM-as-Judge)
topics.summary: How to evaluate LLM features beyond RAG: golden sets, intent accuracy, tool-choice checks, LLM-as-judge rubrics, and gating deploys on scores.
topics.whatIs:
LLM evaluation is the test suite for behaviour you cannot assert with equals. A classifier is right or wrong; a chat reply is good, acceptable or bad along several dimensions. Evaluation turns that into numbers you can track: a golden set of inputs with expected outcomes, a scoring method per dimension, and a script that runs it all after every change.

There are three kinds of checks. Deterministic checks, where the expected output is exact: the intent label, the tool called, the JSON schema, the presence of a required phrase. Rubric checks, where an LLM judge scores the output against written criteria. Human review, sampled, to calibrate the judge and catch what the rubric missed.

For this site the deterministic checks are the valuable ones. Intent accuracy over a labelled set of questions, the fixed contact sentence appearing verbatim, no em dashes in the output, replies under the length limit when a card is shown. Each of those was a real bug once.
topics.why:
Without evaluation every prompt change is a guess and every model upgrade is a gamble. Vendors update models, tweak defaults and deprecate versions; a feature that worked in March can quietly degrade in June. A golden set run in CI is how you find out before users do.

It is also the strongest signal of seniority in AI engineering. Anyone can demo a chatbot. Showing a table where intent accuracy went from 84 to 96 percent after a prompt change, with the failures that remain listed, is engineering.
how: Build a golden set: 50 to 200 inputs covering every intent, edge cases, follow-ups, off-topic and adversarial inputs. Label each with the expected intent, tool, required phrases or a reference answer.
Deterministic scorers first: exact match on labels, schema validation, regex for required or banned patterns, length limits. These are free and unambiguous.

LLM-as-judge for quality: a rubric with binary questions ('Is the answer supported by the context?', 'Does it address the question?', 'Is the tone professional?'), scored by a model, with the rubric versioned alongside the prompt.
Calibrate the judge: hand-score 30 outputs, compare with the judge, fix the rubric until agreement is high.
Run on every change and store results with the prompt version, model name and date. Diff the failures, not only the averages.
Gate deploys: a change that drops any metric below its floor does not ship without a human looking at the failing cases.
pitfalls: Golden sets that only contain happy paths. The value is in the edge cases: follow-ups, typos, off-topic, injection attempts, empty input.
Using the judge for things a regex can check. Deterministic scorers are free, exact and never drift.
A judge rubric nobody calibrated. If the judge and a human disagree 30 percent of the time, the metric is noise.
Watching the average while the same five cases fail every run. Fix the specific failures; they are usually one bug.
Evaluating once before launch. Models and data change; the set is only useful if it runs on every change.
useCases: Gating prompt changes and model upgrades in CI
Measuring intent-classification accuracy for a chat UI
Checking that agents pick the right tool for each request
Comparing two models on cost, latency and quality for the same task
Reporting quality to stakeholders with numbers instead of demos

qa.q: What is a golden set?
qa.a: A fixed collection of inputs with expected outcomes that represents what the feature must handle: every intent, edge cases, adversarial inputs and real user questions from logs. It is the unit-test suite of an LLM feature, rerun on every change and extended whenever a production failure is found.

qa.q: When is LLM-as-judge appropriate?
qa.a: When the quality dimension cannot be checked deterministically: faithfulness to a context, relevance, tone, completeness. Write the rubric as binary questions, calibrate against human scores, and keep it for release decisions only alongside deterministic metrics. Never use it for things a regex or an equality check can decide.

qa.q: How do you evaluate intent classification on this site?
qa.a: A labelled set of questions per intent, including tricky ones like a follow-up about a specific project that must be 'general' rather than 'projects'. The score is plain accuracy plus a confusion view showing which intents get mixed up. Most errors were between 'projects' and 'general', which led to an explicit rule in the prompt.

qa.q: How do you evaluate a model upgrade?
qa.a: Run the same golden set on both models and compare every metric plus cost and latency per call. An upgrade that improves quality by one point and doubles latency is not an upgrade for a chat product. Look at the specific cases that flipped from pass to fail; those are the regressions users will hit.

qa.q: How big should the set be?
qa.a: Big enough that every rule in the prompt has at least a few cases exercising it, and every production bug you have fixed has a regression case. Fifty cases catch most problems for a focused feature; a few hundred for a product with many intents and tools. Coverage matters more than size.

qa.q: How is this different from RAG evaluation?
qa.a: RAG evaluation measures retrieval and faithfulness to retrieved context. App evaluation covers everything else the product promises: the right intent label, the right tool, the required phrasing, length and style limits, refusals and safety. A RAG product needs both sets.

topics.usedIn: Every rule in this site's system prompt, from the intent mapping to the fixed contact sentence and the punctuation rule, exists because a specific case failed once. Those cases are the golden set. The voice agent's planned evaluation milestone adds per-stage latency and cost to the same kind of table.

topics.title: Deploying AI Apps (FastAPI, Docker, Traefik)
topics.summary: How this site is deployed: multi-stage Docker build, FastAPI serving the React app and API, Traefik with automatic TLS, and GitHub Actions.
topics.whatIs:
Deploying an AI app is deploying a web app plus three extra concerns: a model that takes seconds to load, API keys that must never be committed, and calls to paid services that need timeouts and fallbacks. Everything else is ordinary backend engineering, and that is the point: the AI part is a small piece of a system that has to be reliable in the usual ways.

This site runs as one container on a shared VPS. A multi-stage Dockerfile builds the React frontend with Node, then copies the compiled files into a Python image where FastAPI serves them at the root and the API under /api. Traefik, already running on the server for other projects, routes the domain to the container and manages the TLS certificate. A GitHub Actions workflow SSHes in on every push and runs docker compose up with a rebuild.

The decision that mattered most was not adding infrastructure the server did not need. It already had Traefik owning ports 80 and 443 for another site, so a separate Nginx and certbot setup would have conflicted. Joining the existing Docker network with the right labels took one compose file.
topics.why:
A model that only runs on your laptop is a notebook, not a product. Recruiters and clients click the link. Deployment is also where the cost and reliability questions become real: what happens when OpenAI times out, when two requests arrive during model load, when a key leaks into a log.

For a career in AI engineering, shipping is the proof. Knowing Docker, reverse proxies, TLS, environment secrets and CI/CD is what turns a prototype into something a business can depend on, and it is what most AI demos lack.
how: Serve one process: FastAPI mounts the built frontend as static files and exposes the API, so there is one container, one port and no CORS in production.
Multi-stage Dockerfile: a Node stage runs the frontend build, a slim Python stage installs requirements and copies only the compiled assets. The final image has no Node in it.
Load the model at import time, once, and consider baking the model weights into the image so a fresh container does not download them on first start.
Secrets through environment variables from a .env file on the server that is never committed. The compose file reads it; the code reads os.environ.
Traefik labels on the service declare the host rule and the certificate resolver. Traefik issues and renews the Let's Encrypt certificate automatically.
CI/CD: a GitHub Actions job with a dedicated deploy-only SSH key pulls the repo on the server and runs docker compose up -d --build. Rollback is checking out the previous commit and rerunning.
topics.code:
# Dockerfile (multi-stage)
FROM node:20-alpine AS frontend-build
WORKDIR /app/frontend
COPY frontend/package.json frontend/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY frontend/ ./
RUN npm run build

FROM python:3.11-slim AS backend
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY main.py knowledge_base.txt ./
COPY learn-hub ./learn-hub
RUN python learn-hub/build.py            # static site generated at build time
COPY --from=frontend-build /app/frontend/dist ./frontend/dist
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

# docker-compose.yml (excerpt): join the existing Traefik network
# services:
#   backend:
#     build: .
#     env_file: .env
#     networks: [n8n_default]
#     labels:
#       - traefik.enable=true
#       - traefik.http.routers.portfolio.rule=Host(`abdurrehmanafzal.cloud`)
#       - traefik.http.routers.portfolio.tls.certresolver=mytlschallenge
#       - traefik.http.services.portfolio.loadbalancer.server.port=8000
# networks:
#   n8n_default:
#     external: true
pitfalls: Committing the .env file or printing keys in logs. Use environment variables, add .env to .gitignore before the first commit, and rotate any key that was ever pushed.
Downloading model weights on every container start. It adds a slow cold start and a dependency on a third-party host during deploy; bake them into the image or a volume.
No timeout on LLM calls. A hung upstream call ties up a worker forever. Set client timeouts and return a fallback.
Running a second reverse proxy on a server that already has one. Check what owns ports 80 and 443 before planning.
A deploy pipeline that cannot roll back. Tag images or keep the previous commit one command away.
useCases: Portfolio and demo sites that must stay up for recruiters
Internal AI tools on a single VPS alongside other services
Client chatbots delivered as one container with a compose file
Voice agents on their own subdomain with a separate container
Any FastAPI service that wraps a model and a frontend

qa.q: Why serve the frontend from FastAPI instead of a separate host?
qa.a: One container, one domain, no CORS configuration and no second deployment to keep in sync. For a small product the simplicity wins. I would split them when the frontend needs a CDN or when the two teams deploy on different schedules.

qa.q: Why Traefik instead of Nginx?
qa.a: The server already ran Traefik for another site, and it owned ports 80 and 443. Adding Nginx would have conflicted. Traefik also issues and renews TLS certificates automatically from labels on the container, which removed certbot from the setup entirely. The right proxy is the one already running.

qa.q: How do you handle the model load time?
qa.a: Load at import so the first request does not pay for it, and keep a health endpoint that only reports ready once the model is loaded so the proxy does not route traffic early. Baking weights into the image avoids the network download. For heavier models I would use a startup event and a readiness probe.

qa.q: What does the CI/CD pipeline do?
qa.a: On push to the deploy branch, a GitHub Actions job connects to the VPS over SSH with a dedicated deploy-only key, pulls the latest commit and runs docker compose up with a rebuild. The build happens on the server. It is deliberately simple; the hard part was the key management and making the script idempotent.

qa.q: How do you keep costs predictable in production?
qa.a: A cheap default model, token limits on replies and history, timeouts, rate limits per client, and a spend alert on the provider dashboard. The voice agent adds a hard session cap. None of this is AI-specific; it is the same discipline as any metered API.

qa.q: What would you add for a higher-traffic version?
qa.a: Multiple uvicorn workers or replicas behind the proxy, the model served by a separate process so web workers stay light, a Redis cache for repeated questions, structured logging with request ids, and metrics for latency per stage. Only when measured traffic demands it.

The voice agent is planned for its own subdomain with the same pattern.

topics.title: Latency & Cost Control for LLM Apps
topics.summary: Practical ways to make LLM features fast and cheap: streaming, model choice, token budgets, caching, timeouts, fallbacks and measuring per stage.
topics.whatIs:
Every LLM call costs money per token and takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. Latency and cost control is the set of decisions that keep both inside a budget: which model, how many tokens in and out, what to cache, what to stream, when to give up and what to do when the provider is slow or down.

The two are linked. Fewer tokens in the prompt means less cost and faster first token. A smaller model is cheaper and faster. Streaming does not reduce cost but makes the same latency feel much shorter. Caching removes both for repeated questions.

On this site, the choices were: a small model, five short chunks instead of the whole knowledge base, a bounded history, a fixed reply for the contact intent, lead extraction only after a cheap regex pre-filter and only in a background task, and a keyword fallback when OpenAI fails. The voice agent adds streaming at every stage and a hard session timer.
topics.why:
Users leave slow products and businesses cancel expensive ones. A chat feature that costs more per conversation than the revenue it protects will be switched off. A voice agent that pauses three seconds before every reply will never be used twice.

Cost is also the question every client asks second, right after 'does it work'. Being able to say 'about this much per conversation, here is how I measured it and here is the lever if it needs to be lower' is what separates an engineer from a demo builder.
how: Measure first: log tokens in, tokens out, latency to first token and total latency for every call, tagged by feature. You cannot optimise what you have not measured.
Pick the smallest model that passes your evaluation set. Try the cheap model first and upgrade only where the eval shows it fails.
Budget the prompt: cap retrieved context, trim history, keep the system prompt lean. Input tokens are usually the biggest cost in RAG.
Cap the output with max_tokens and ask for short replies in the prompt. Output tokens cost more and take longer.
Stream responses to the UI so the user reads while the model writes. For voice, stream text to speech sentence by sentence.

Cache: identical questions can return a stored answer; provider-side prompt caching cuts the cost of a long, stable system prompt. Set timeouts and a fallback path so a slow provider degrades the experience instead of breaking it.
topics.code:
import time, hashlib, functools
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(timeout=15.0, max_retries=1)      # never hang a worker

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=512)
def _cached(key: str, prompt: str) -> str:
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini", max_tokens=300,       # cap the expensive side
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return r.choices[0].message.content

def answer(question: str, context: str, fallback) -> dict:
    prompt = f"Context:\n{context}\n\nAnswer briefly: {question}"
    key = hashlib.sha256(prompt.encode()).hexdigest()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        text, source = _cached(key, prompt), "llm"
    except Exception as e:                        # timeout, outage, quota
        text, source = fallback(question), f"fallback:{type(e).__name__}"
    ms = round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)
    print({"source": source, "latency_ms": ms, "prompt_chars": len(prompt)})
    return {"text": text, "source": source, "latency_ms": ms}

# Streaming for the UI: yield tokens as they arrive
def stream(prompt: str):
    with client.chat.completions.stream(model="gpt-4o-mini",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]) as s:
        for event in s:
            if event.type == "content.delta":
                yield event.delta
pitfalls: Defaulting to the biggest model. Most product tasks pass on a small model; the eval set, not instinct, should decide.
Stuffing the whole document into the prompt 'to be safe'. It multiplies cost and makes answers worse.
No timeout, so one slow upstream call blocks a worker and the queue behind it.
Measuring average latency only. Users feel the p95; report percentiles and time to first token.
Caching without a key that includes the context. A cached answer from an old knowledge base is a stale answer.
useCases: Chat products with a per-conversation cost target

Public demos that must survive traffic spikes without a surprise bill
Any feature that needs a graceful answer when the provider is down

qa.q: What is the single biggest cost lever in a RAG app?
qa.a: Input tokens, meaning the retrieved context and history sent on every call. Retrieving five tight chunks instead of twenty, and trimming history to the last few turns, usually cuts cost by more than switching models. Output tokens matter next; cap them and ask for short replies.

qa.q: Does streaming make the model faster?
qa.a: No, total time is the same. It makes the product feel faster because the user sees the first words within a few hundred milliseconds instead of waiting for the whole reply. In voice it is essential: speech starts on the first sentence while the rest is still being generated.

qa.q: How do you choose between gpt-4o-mini and a larger model?
qa.a: Run the golden set on both. If the small model passes, use it; it is many times cheaper and faster. Where it fails, check whether a better prompt or better retrieval fixes it before paying for the larger model. Route by task if needed: small model for classification and chat, larger for the rare complex question.

qa.q: What should happen when the LLM provider is down?
qa.a: The product should still answer something useful. This site falls back to a keyword-based responder over the same real data, so a visitor gets correct facts in plainer prose instead of an error. Timeouts, limited retries and a fallback path are the minimum for anything public.

qa.q: How does prompt caching work?
qa.a: Providers can cache the processed prefix of a prompt, so a long, stable system prompt and reference text are billed at a lower rate and processed faster on subsequent calls. Structure prompts so the stable part comes first and the variable part last, and the cache hits often.

qa.q: How do you measure cost per conversation?
qa.a: Log tokens in and out per call with the model name, multiply by the price per token, and sum per session id. Report the distribution, not just the mean, because a few long conversations dominate. Then set an alert on daily spend so a bug or an attack shows up the same day.
